title: Refine Story research prompt using sibling briefs
description: Review sibling prompts under ai/findings/Story, identify useful ideas and independent improvements, and edit only ai/findings/Story/astra/prompt.md. Preserve the pre-alpha stance and improve research quality and decision usefulness without inflating scope. Do not execute the research.
design:
# Research brief: Story parity, ergonomics, and opportunities to be better

You are researching Story, re-frame2's component and application-state development tool. Produce an independent, carefully evidenced product and technical assessment, with concrete recommendations, in this repository's `ai/findings/Story/astra/` directory.

The user wants Story to have feature parity with Storybook and comparable JavaScript and non-JavaScript alternatives, while taking full advantage of re-frame2's strengths, idioms, and ethos. Answer two questions:

1. How can we test how close Story actually is to that objective today?
2. Where could Story be meaningfully more powerful, more ergonomic, and more productive for programmers and their AI assistants?

Investigate and write the report. Recommendations need evidence and judgment; a catalogue of features or an aspirational roadmap alone will not answer these questions.

The primary audience is a programmer building a re-frame2 SPA and choosing a component/state workshop. Distinguish an experienced Storybook user new to Story, a returning application or design-system maintainer, and their AI assistant. State the framework knowledge each journey assumes; source-code familiarity acquired during this research must not silently become an onboarding prerequisite.

## Project posture

> Posture is that we are pre-alpha and focused on elegance, power and a masterpiece.
> But we are not over-engineering or gold plating. Also, we trust the programmer.
> We're trying to facilitate high productivity for them (and the AI they use) via a
> library with excellent ergonomics and low friction. We don't need to litigate every
> last fine detail and drown in the minutiae.

Apply this posture to the analysis and the recommendations. The goal is an excellent workshop for creating SPAs: minimal, expressive APIs; useful defaults; composable capabilities; short feedback loops; and excellent tools. Pre-alpha permits simplifying or replacing awkward designs. It does not justify unreliable everyday workflows.

Feature parity is a serious objective. Start by understanding what users can accomplish with the alternatives. Do not quietly narrow parity to the areas where Story already looks strong, or label an inconvenient omission a deliberate divergence without a reason. At the same time, parity does not require reproducing another product's API, implementation, plugin count, commercial service, or accumulated complexity. Explain which outcomes matter, how Story can provide them idiomatically, and which differences we should consciously accept.

Look for improvements that remove concepts, configuration, repeated work, and unnecessary friction as well as improvements that add capability. Do not recommend a framework within the framework, a new policy system, or a large infrastructure project when a small primitive, better integration, or clearer workflow would solve the problem.

## Working scope and deliverables

The repository root is `C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2`. Resolve paths against the checkout you actually inspect. Read applicable `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` instructions and run `bd prime`. Use beads for task tracking as required by the repository. Read relevant existing beads, including later notes and rulings, to avoid proposing already-resolved work; treat their factual claims as leads to verify independently.

Write:

- `ai/findings/Story/astra/report.md`: the main report and recommendations.
- `ai/findings/Story/astra/parity-matrix.md`: the evidence-backed comparison, linked from the report.
- `ai/findings/Story/astra/evaluation-plan.md`: the practical, repeatable evaluation protocol and results obtained during this research.
- Supporting evidence under `ai/findings/Story/astra/evidence/` only where it improves reproducibility or keeps the main documents readable.

Keep this `prompt.md` intact. Preserve existing unrelated work. Findings under `ai/` are local artifacts; follow the repository's rule against adding them to Git. This is a research assignment, not authorization to implement recommended product changes or turn every comparison row into a new bead. Use isolated scratch fixtures for experiments where needed, following the repository's checkout and gate instructions. Record implementation proposals in the report and link existing beads rather than creating a speculative backlog.

Include the research timestamp with timezone, the inspected repository commit, relevant local changes, competitor versions, and exact test environments. If the checkout moves during research, pin material observations to the revision examined and check consequential drift before concluding. An unavailable browser, credential, dependency, or service is a limitation to report, not evidence of either parity or a product defect.

This brief incorporates methodological ideas from the sibling `grok/prompt.md` and `fable/prompt.md`. Their claims are not evidence. Establish your comparison criteria and initial assessment before reading any sibling reports; if you later compare conclusions, identify disagreements and verify them rather than voting between reports. Disclose that synthesis separately from your initial findings.

## 1. Establish what Story actually is today

Build a concise map from user-facing capability to public API, implementation, test coverage, and a runnable example. Useful starting points, to verify rather than treat as an exhaustive or authoritative inventory:

- `README.md`, `docs/story/`, and `docs/story/api/`.
- `spec/007-Stories.md`, `spec/Principles.md`, `spec/Ownership.md`, and relevant frame, schema, instrumentation, and state-machine contracts.
- `tools/story/README.md`, `tools/story/spec/README.md`, and the linked vision, principles, design rationale, API, runtime, authoring, testing, and UI contracts. Engage explicitly with the parity-and-surpass thesis in `018-Story-UI-North-Star.md`: does Story deliver it, and is it the right thesis? Use its user stories and existing budgets as inputs to challenge. Pull `017-Testing-Story.md` and other capability contracts when a journey needs them; a complete spec read-through is unnecessary.
- `tools/story/src/`, `tools/story/test/`, and `tools/story/testbeds/`, including `login_form`, `counter_with_stories`, and `fresco_counter`.
- `examples/patterns/nine_states/` and other real application examples where they illuminate everyday SPA work.
- `tools/story-mcp/`, `docs/story/api/mcp-surface.md`, and the Story references under `skills/re-frame2/references/tooling/`.
- The Xray, pair/MCP, renderer, and framework code actually used by the workflows under review.
- Current build scripts, `implementation/package.json`, compiler configuration, and the CI jobs that really exercise these paths.

Documentation, test names, a green aggregate job, and a public function's existence do not individually establish a working user journey. Trace important claims through the actual integration and exercise representative paths. Distinguish implemented behavior, documented contracts, historical proposals, and known limitations. Explicitly test prominent parity or superiority claims in the repository; do not repeat them as conclusions.

After drafting your current comparison criteria, consult `tools/story/spec/Feature-Parity-Audit.md`, the feature-set and SOTA-refinement research under `tools/story/spec/findings/`, and `ai/findings/story-review.md` if present. Recheck consequential claims against today's source and relevant bead history. Report material changes from the earlier audit—resolved gaps, remaining gaps, overstated wins, and changed assumptions—with evidence. Do not mechanically rescore every historical row or repeat the implementation review. A prior defect matters here when it invalidates a user outcome; an old finding may already be fixed. Labels such as `CURRENT`, `TARGET`, and `BLOCKED` in specs describe claims or intent, not runtime proof.

Use the current public vocabulary. For example, investigate `:setup`, `:script`, and `story/run`, `story/is`, and `story/explain` at source before copying examples from older documents. Do not mistake a retired spelling or old design for a missing current capability. Likewise, distinguish a subject's authoring substrate from the adapter hosting the Story shell.

## 2. Research a fair comparison set

Browse current primary sources: official documentation, release notes, maintained source repositories, and official examples. Establish the current stable Storybook baseline at the research date; do not inherit an old version number from this repository. Identify experimental or announced capabilities separately from released ones.

Use Storybook as the main comparison. Select a small, justified set of complementary alternatives, normally four to six products in total, including:

- A lighter JavaScript component workshop. Investigate candidates such as Ladle, Histoire, and React Cosmos and select based on current relevance and maintenance.
- An idiomatic Clojure/ClojureScript alternative, such as Portfolio, if its current scope makes it informative.
- At least one non-JavaScript example with a materially different approach: for example Lookbook, Flutter's Widgetbook, SwiftUI previews, or a Phoenix component workshop. Verify suitability and availability before choosing.

These are research candidates, not assertions about their current capabilities. Give the selection rationale and explain the limits of cross-language comparisons. Research adjacent visual testing, browser testing, design review, and agent tooling where they complete a common workflow, without expanding into an exhaustive survey of the whole frontend ecosystem.

Briefly check the ClojureScript lineage, including devcards and workspaces, before describing a familiar idea as a Story invention. Explicitly verify competitors' current agent/MCP/CLI surfaces; neither their absence nor Story's uniqueness is a premise. Follow an additional comparator only when it changes a relevant judgment, test, or recommendation.

For each capability, distinguish built-in support, an official integration, a maintained community integration, a hosted/paid service, and custom application work. Include ordinary, idiomatic integrations in a competitor's strongest practical workflow. Do not compare Story plus its entire ecosystem against an artificially bare competitor. Conversely, do not attribute a separate service's capabilities to an open-source package without naming the dependency, setup burden, and any relevant cost or account requirement. Verify current commercial facts if they affect a recommendation.

Cite direct primary-source URLs near claims, with version or retrieval context. Treat marketing as a claim to investigate. When sources disagree, resolve consequential differences through source inspection or a small experiment and state any remaining uncertainty.

## 3. Define parity in terms of outcomes

Organize the matrix around useful tasks, with feature details underneath them. Cover the following areas at an appropriate depth; split or combine rows to avoid either hiding a major gap or counting a dozen cosmetic variations as a dozen capabilities:

- Getting started in a new or existing application; dependency and build setup; discovery; hot reload; editor navigation; understandable examples and errors.
- Authoring components and application states; args and controls; schemas/types; reusable setup, decorators, fixtures, and composition; source visibility; ordinary application code reuse.
- Real SPA behavior: forms, routing, asynchronous loading, errors and retries, state machines, resources, effects, clocks, external I/O, and controllable test data.
- Isolation, reset, lifecycle cleanup, parallel or side-by-side states, and comparison across supported renderers, themes, viewports, locales, and other meaningful axes.
- Interaction testing, assertions, test discovery, headless and browser execution, debugging failures, deterministic reproduction, recording, and converting a useful scenario into a regression test.
- Visual regression and review: capture, baseline comparison, actionable diffs, and review workflows. A declared-input fingerprint is not a pixel comparison or a visual approval service.
- Accessibility: testing the rendered subject and the usability of the workshop itself. Separate automated checks from keyboard/focus behavior and what still requires human judgment.
- Documentation, examples, API/args explanations, navigation/search, documentation embedding, static publication, deep links, sharing, and composition across projects where relevant.
- Runtime inspection and feedback: events, subscriptions, app state, effects, machines, traces, time travel, and connecting a failure to its cause.
- Extension and integration surfaces; installation and upgrade burden; startup, rebuild, interaction, and larger-catalog behavior; production exclusion of development tooling.
- AI-assisted work: discover, inspect, author, execute, diagnose, revise, and verify through the supported tool/skill/MCP surfaces, using the same artifacts and results as the human UI.

For each meaningful row provide the user outcome and importance; competitor support and requirements; Story's actual behavior and public entry point; supporting evidence; a concrete acceptance test; limitations; and confidence. Make disagreements among contract, implementation, documentation, and everyday usability visible. An undocumented internal route is evidence of technical possibility, not a finished user workflow.

Use separate columns for **capability status** and **evidence strength**. Suggested statuses are complete for the stated scope, partial, absent, intentional divergence, not applicable, and unknown. Evidence can be exercised, source-traced, documented only, or unverified. A supported capability can still be poorly evidenced, and a confirmed gap can have high confidence. Do not force an unverified claim into complete or absent. Describe comparative strengths and discoverability separately rather than awarding Story a special status that makes the matrix incomparable.

Summarize how close Story is by important workflow and capability area, clearly exposing adoption blockers and unknowns. If you calculate a score, show the denominator, weights, exclusions, and how unverified rows affect it; provide a range where warranted. Do not let many minor successes cancel one essential failure, or let a precise percentage conceal a weak evidence base. An honest categorical assessment is preferable to a misleading single number.

## 4. Design and exercise an evaluation that can be repeated

Develop a small benchmark application or use suitable existing fixtures. Include a simple component, a stateful form, and an asynchronous SPA journey. Compare equivalent user outcomes through each tool's idiomatic approach, with comparable assumptions and fixtures. Avoid making competitors adopt re-frame2 internals or requiring Story to copy JavaScript authoring syntax.

Record the initial jobs, acceptance criteria, and relative importance in `evaluation-plan.md` before scoring them. Explain later changes so the rubric cannot quietly move to favor a result. Give jobs stable IDs shared by the matrix, evidence, and recommendations. Keep the method small enough to rerun without this prompt.

Specify a compact set of approximately eight to ten scenarios, adapting this starting set where evidence suggests a better one:

1. Follow the public getting-started instructions literally to reach a useful first story; record stalls, undocumented boot steps, and source-code lookups. Change application code and observe the feedback loop. Distinguish this walkthrough from a real novice-user study.
2. Author a simple props/args-driven component, controls, and reusable variants. Then try increasing one variant's fidelity from pinned inputs or seeded state to real setup events without rewriting the scenario; record what additional behavior the stronger version actually proves.
3. Explore loading, success, empty, validation-error, server-error, and retry states of a real form or data view, with predictable effects and time.
4. Render independent states side by side; interact, reset, and switch variants without cross-contamination or stale asynchronous results. Check relevant isolation boundaries such as CSS, focus/portals, global state, and external effects; frame-local state alone does not prove whole-page isolation.
5. Exercise supported theme, viewport, locale, and renderer combinations and find a layout or interaction defect. State exactly which combinations were verified.
6. Record or author a behavior, turn it into an automated test, and rerun it locally and through the appropriate CI path.
7. Diagnose a deliberately introduced application failure, find the causal event/state/effect, preserve it as a failing regression variant, then correct the fault and rerun. Keep assertions capable of detecting the original fault. Distinguish state restoration from replaying external effects.
8. Detect an intentional visual and accessibility regression; explain baseline ownership and human review boundaries.
9. Publish or share a useful reproduction/documentation page and open it in a fresh context, identifying what state and dependencies do or do not travel with it.
10. Have an AI assistant discover a scenario, run it, inspect the same failure a human sees, propose or author a minimal change, and verify the result through supported tools.

For each scenario specify prerequisites, steps, expected observations, failure signals, the simplest adequate verification method, and what proves completion. Separate the proposed reusable protocol from the measurements you actually obtained.

During this research, execute a small but consequential subset on Story and at least the main Storybook baseline where the environment permits: an authoring/controls journey, a stateful asynchronous interaction/test journey, and a failure-diagnosis journey. Inspect the real rendered browser UI when judging interaction or usability. Use source and documentation for breadth and deeper execution for the claims that could change the recommendations. If a comparison cannot run, give the exact limitation and the smallest experiment needed next; do not invent timings or imply execution.

Measure what helps a programmer decide: manual setup, files and concepts touched, repeated declarations, time to first useful result, feedback latency, recovery from an ordinary mistake, reproducibility, clarity of failure evidence, and human/agent handoffs. Report actual timings with hardware, versions, cold/warm state, and sample count. Small exploratory samples are observations, not general performance claims. Code examples and annotated workflow comparisons often reveal ergonomics better than raw line counts.

Explain how to repeat the evaluation: prerequisites and commands, a short smoke subset, deeper checks for affected workflows, and the observed or estimated cost of each. Identify what invalidates a row—relevant code, docs, integration, or competitor-version changes—and retain unaffected evidence. Separate deterministic checks suitable for existing automation from usability judgments requiring a person. Reuse existing parity budgets where applicable. Propose a lightweight rerun cadence or triggers, not a new permanent gate for every row.

Use a few deliberate failures or negative controls to establish that a claimed test detects the defect in question. A headless success cannot prove DOM interaction, and a skipped browser test cannot prove parity. Read the runner's actual exit status and coverage conditions; follow the repository's absolute-path, checkout-verification, and unique ignored-log instructions for gates. Prefer existing harnesses. A new permanent benchmark service or a broad testing-platform rewrite is not required for this research.

## 5. Imagine better workflows and try to disprove the advantage

Generate candidate improvements from real development friction and from what re-frame2 makes unusually simple. Investigate, without presuming superiority:

- Named application states as reusable data that can serve a workshop, documentation, tests, reproductions, and agent tools without parallel definitions.
- Frames as a basis for reliable, simultaneous state exploration and repeatable experiments.
- Events, subscriptions, effects, resources, and machines as a shared vocabulary for driving behavior and explaining why a view looks as it does.
- Schema-derived controls, representative data, and useful state exploration without a second configuration language or uncontrolled combinatorial expansion.
- Xray and trace/epoch evidence as a way to move from a visible failure to a causal explanation with fewer manual steps.
- One productive human/AI loop with inspectable artifacts, clear results, and minimal translation between interfaces.
- Composition that makes rich scenarios easier to express while keeping the common case short; improvements obtained by deleting, consolidating, or improving defaults.

For each promising idea, show a concrete before/after authoring or debugging workflow, a small idiomatic API/data sketch where helpful, and a falsifiable hypothesis about user benefit. Label proposed APIs clearly; verify any example presented as working today. Distinguish an existing but undiscoverable strength from an integration gap and from a new capability.

Compare the idea with the strongest practical competitor solution, including suitable integrations. Explain what re-frame2 contributes and what it costs: additional concepts, coupling, configuration, runtime/tooling weight, and maintenance. Consider the limits of data-shaped artifacts, state isolation, and replay when real external I/O or non-serializable behavior is involved. Do not turn those limits into elaborate machinery without a concrete user need.

Synthesize a concise product thesis: which users should prefer Story, for which jobs, and why its few underlying concepts make those jobs easier. Illustrate it with two or three concrete future workflows, distinguishing capabilities already available from the smallest missing pieces. A useful advantage can be a common task made substantially easier; novelty or a task impossible elsewhere is not required.

Select roughly three to five opportunities worth pursuing, and explain why other plausible ideas should wait or be declined. It is acceptable to find that an alternative is more ergonomic, or that Story already has the right capability and needs better presentation. Do not manufacture novelty or claim competitors cannot do something merely because their core documentation does not mention it. Separate benefits supplied by re-frame2 itself from benefits Story makes accessible, and check that its simplest component workflow remains pleasant alongside its richer SPA workflows.

## 6. Make recommendations that can guide decisions

Rank a short set of recommendations by user impact, evidence, reach across workflows, and implementation/maintenance cost. Separate:

- Essential parity gaps or correctness failures that obstruct ordinary adoption.
- Existing capabilities whose discoverability, integration, or ergonomics need improvement.
- Distinctive improvements that earn their complexity through demonstrable user benefit.
- Deliberate differences, low-value imitations, and work to defer.

For each recommendation provide the concrete problem and affected user; evidence and confidence; the smallest coherent change; a before/after example; likely owning surfaces; rough effort and dependencies; and a testable acceptance criterion linked to the affected job IDs. State what it removes or simplifies as well as what it adds. Cite related beads and relevant current decisions, without treating past decisions as substitutes for fresh analysis. Where a recommendation challenges an existing design, state the tradeoff and the evidence that warrants revisiting it.

Avoid a long task inventory. Cluster symptoms with a common remedy, and separate measured defects from research hypotheses. Offer a sensible sequence for the next few improvements, with a clear stopping point and an explanation of what would change the ordering.

## Report shape and quality bar

Lead `report.md` with the answer: how close Story is for the named users, which essential journeys still prevent a credible parity claim, the product thesis, and the first improvement you would choose. Then present the relevant evidence, material changes from prior research, workflow comparisons, strongest opportunities, recommended sequence, and remaining uncertainties. Link the detailed matrix and evaluation plan instead of duplicating them. Keep the main report decision-focused; put bulky receipts in the evidence directory. Prefer useful depth over encyclopedic coverage.

The report must make it easy to distinguish:

- What exists and works now.
- What is supported only by source inspection or documentation.
- What failed, and under which conditions.
- What remains untested or unknown.
- What is proposed, why it would help, and how that benefit would be tested.

Before finishing, challenge your own conclusions. Did you verify the loudest claims? Did you compare complete workflows fairly? Did the tests exercise the relevant browser or runtime? Did you mistake a hosted service for a built-in feature, a fingerprint for visual regression, or an existing primitive for a user-friendly finished workflow? Have you recommended the smallest powerful design, and have you explicitly declined attractive work that does not earn its cost?

Deliver a report that lets the user make a few well-founded product decisions and gives the team a practical way to measure progress toward parity and superiority over time.

Added audience and knowledge assumptions, literal first-hour walkthroughs, fidelity progression, frame versus whole-page isolation checks, preserved failing regression scenarios, explicit unknown status, current competitor AI verification, and attribution of framework versus tool benefits. Retained bounded comparator and scenario sets, separate capability/evidence columns, and optional honest scoring. title: Timer: preserve elapsed when duration drops below a pending tick
description:
Preserve already measured elapsed time when a running Timer's duration is shortened below it. An accepted pending tick currently clamps elapsed downward to the new duration, and a later slider increase then restarts a timer that should remain complete. Stop that tick without reducing elapsed; retain recorded-time sampling and the generation guard.

Ownership and review identity
- Slice: examples_core. Owner: examples/core/seven_guis/timer/core.cljs.
- Baseline: 9e8ca973767f4ecff455421e48e1765d59783261. Revalidated current source in the 2026-09-13 read-only review; no source edits.
- SOURCE_ROOT=C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2; WORKTREE_ROOT=(none; read-only review).
- Split from finding 2 of rf2-fzbj.18, which remains unchanged. Its title fence is retained: remediation is held until Mike rules who remediates rf2-fzbj. This issue records an independent finding and does not authorize dispatch or source remediation.

Evidence and reproducer
Source: core.cljs:132-152, especially line 143 `(min (+ elapsed-ms observed) duration-ms)`; duration edits at 163-183 preserve elapsed but keep the pending tick generation accepted. Restart eligibility at 166-170 then reads the rewound elapsed value. Namespace rules at 20-24 describe the reduced target filling the bar and Reset clearing elapsed. The already-completed timer's set-duration path also preserves elapsed.

Drive the actual handlers with the existing recordable :rf/time-ms coeffect:
1. t=0, [:timer/initialise]: elapsed=0, duration=10000, generation=0.
2. t=5000, [:timer/tick 0]: elapsed=5000, with the next tick scheduled.
3. t=5050, [:timer/set-duration 1000]: elapsed remains 5000 and duration becomes 1000, so the bar is full.
4. t=5100, the pending [:timer/tick 0] arrives: actual elapsed becomes 1000 and no further tick is scheduled.
5. t=5200, [:timer/set-duration 3000]: actual generation becomes 1 and a fresh [:timer/tick 1] is scheduled, because 3000 exceeds the incorrectly reduced 1000.

Expected: step 4 preserves elapsed=5000 and stops scheduling. Step 5 stays stopped because duration=3000 remains below elapsed=5000. A later increase above 5000 may re-arm once from a fresh time baseline. Reset still zeroes elapsed.

Control: first complete the timer at elapsed=10000, then reduce duration to 1000. Elapsed stays 10000 because there is no pending tick to perform the downward min. Thus ordinary slider semantics currently depend on whether a callback remains in flight.

Impact
The displayed elapsed label loses already observed time and a subsequent slider edit can resume a timer that should remain complete. This is the central competing timer/user interaction that the Timer example is intended to teach, rather than a malformed programmer-only event payload.

Suggested repair
For an accepted tick whose elapsed-ms is already >= duration-ms, preserve elapsed and stop scheduling instead of running the downward min clamp. An explicit set-duration stop transition is also valid if it preserves the same invariant and accounts for pending generations. Keep recorded observed-time accounting, stale-generation rejection, the fresh re-arm baseline, and intentional clamping of a forward tick at its original deadline. No general timer abstraction is needed.

Acceptance criteria
1. The exact 0/5000/5050/5100 sequence preserves elapsed=5000 after the pending tick and emits no follow-up schedule.
2. Increasing duration to 3000 stays stopped; increasing above 5000 re-arms exactly one generation and measures from the re-arm event.
3. A mid-run reduction and an already-stopped reduction preserve already measured elapsed consistently.
4. Extend implementation/core/test/re_frame/example_generation_guard_cljs_test.cljs with this interaction. Preserve its delayed-sample, forward-deadline clamp, stale-generation, Reset, and re-arm baseline cases. Keep examples test-free (rf2-8cevm).

Validation and limits
Freshly ran bb C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2/ai/surface-review-20260913/examples_core/probe-examples_core-1.clj against the current source. Captured exit 0, verified the absolute source-root banner, and confirmed probe/log/exit artifacts are ignored. The probe extracts and evaluates the actual Timer event-handler forms with process-local db and controlled coeffects; it confirms each state above, the stopped-timer control, and the incorrect schedule after raising duration to 3000. No dispatcher, host timer, adapter, browser, compilation, server, or broad gate was used. Framework regression source and runner selection were inspected; those suites were not executed or called green. Probe success confirms the defect rather than a repair.

Known history and duplicate disposition
- rf2-fzbj.18 is the unchanged aggregate report containing this and the independent Cells finding; its newest three history entries preserve the open fenced status. Splitting this finding does not remove the ownership hold.
- rf2-4s8g is closed and its newest history/close reason confirms the prior callback-count defect was repaired by recorded time and sampled-at-ms (PR #9260). Current source retains that repair. This issue is the distinct duration-reduction/pending-tick interaction; it does not reopen the deliberate forward-deadline clamp decision.
- Live all-status title searches for Timer and description searches for timer/set-duration and the exact source path found no dedicated open issue for this outcome.
notes:
REMEDIATED — PR #9762 (branch worker/excore-a), 2026-09-13. This is finding 2 of rf2-fzbj.18; both beads are closed by the same change. Re-verified at tip before fixing: the tick still ran the downward `min` clamp and the reproducer still rewound elapsed, exactly as filed.

THE FIX. The accepted tick in examples/core/seven_guis/timer/core.cljs now computes `(max elapsed-ms (min (+ elapsed-ms observed) duration-ms))`. The intentional forward-deadline clamp is preserved — a late sample still lands exactly on the duration and never overruns — while a tick that finds the slider has pulled the deadline below time already measured holds elapsed and stops scheduling instead of clamping down to the new target. Measured time is never handed back; only Reset zeroes it. Observed-time accounting, the stale-generation guard and the fresh re-arm baseline are untouched, and no general timer abstraction was introduced.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA, each pinned in implementation/core/test/re_frame/example_generation_guard_cljs_test.cljs (examples stay test-free per rf2-8cevm):
1. The exact 0 / 5000 / 5050 / 5100 sequence leaves elapsed at 5000 after the pending tick, with no follow-up scheduled.
2. Raising the duration to 3000 keeps it stopped at generation 0 with nothing scheduled; raising it to 8000 re-arms exactly one generation, and the first resumed sample counts the 100ms since the drag (5100), not the interval since the last tick.
3. The already-finished reduction obeys the same rule: a timer completed at 10000 keeps its elapsed when the duration is cut to 1000 and again to 3000, and stays finished.
4. The file's existing delayed-sample, original-deadline clamp, stale-generation, Reset and re-arm baseline cases are unchanged and green.

EVIDENCE (captured exit codes, on the branch's final rebased base): `npm run test:cljs` from implementation/ exit 0 — 12024 tests / 59830 assertions, 0 failures 0 errors, compile 0 warnings (CI job `cljs`); `node implementation/scripts/check-examples-compile.cjs` over its 58 derived build ids including examples/timer (CI job `cljs-examples-compile`). RED-THEN-GREEN: with the tests held fixed and only the example source reverted to its pre-fix blob, the focused run read exit 1 — elapsed rewound to 1000 and a re-arm at 3000, the filed defect — then exit 0 with the fix restored, at the same 24 tests / 172 assertions both times; restore verified by blob hash.

TEACHING TEXT updated: the namespace's rules now say that dragging the duration below elapsed fills the bar while elapsed keeps the time it has measured, and that the timer picks up again when the slider goes back up past elapsed; the `:timer/set-duration` docstring says what a live tick does when the target now sits below elapsed.

NOT BUILT, deliberately: the alternative "explicit stop transition in set-duration". The tick-side fix already preserves the invariant on every path including a tick already in flight, so a second stop path would duplicate it and add a second place for the rule to drift.

title: Plain SSR example returns before its article request settles
description:
Wait for the page's article request to reach a terminal outcome before the plain SSR example snapshots state and renders. Use the existing event/effect and request-lifecycle facilities, with a bounded failure/deadline outcome; keep the demonstration small.

Remediation fence: this finding is split from rf2-fzbj.37 F1. Preserve [FENCE: until Mike rules who remediates rf2-fzbj]. This review authorizes reporting, not implementation or fixer dispatch.

Ownership and revision
- Slice examples_capabilities; examples/capabilities/ssr/ssr/core.cljc:137-157, 276-293, 331-361; associated README.md:61-86.
- Baseline 9e8ca973767f4ecff455421e48e1765d59783261; reviewed HEAD 4df6a3303c68c77ced1f84ce92178bed1d7f7879. Owned paths are unchanged between these revisions and in the working tree.
- SOURCE_ROOT=C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2. WORKTREE_ROOT=(none; read-only review).

Trigger and actual behavior
The real server-init returns :rf.http/managed GET /api/articles. make-frame drains synchronous event work, then handle-request immediately reads final-db, builds the payload and destroys the request frame. The JVM transport uses HttpClient/sendAsync (implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/transport_jvm.cljc:287), so frame construction does not establish HTTP completion. Then the probe releases the reply and closes the server and executor.

title: machines: preserve successor timers when delay resolution replaces the frame
description:
Recheck the captured frame incarnation immediately after resolving an :after delay, before reserving its timer-table slot. The current schedule-after-timer! continuation can overwrite a same-id successor frame's independently armed timer, then remove its own replacement sentinel; the successor loses its live timeout and its host handle becomes orphaned. Reuse the existing owner-gone? predicate and attempt-token protocol; no public API or new ownership mechanism is needed.

Ownership and revision
- Surface: impl_machines, implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/timer.cljc.
- Baseline: 9e8ca973767f4ecff455421e48e1765d59783261. Witness ran against 50abcab5ce674e5107b34834ebbfd81d1af7e2cd; git diff against the baseline showed no owned-source changes.
- SOURCE_ROOT=C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2. WORKTREE_ROOT=(none; read-only review).
- Fresh review finding under rf2-gwye. Review delivery only; no fixer is dispatched and no production remediation is authorized by this bead.

Confirmed P2 defect and source
1. timer.cljc:643-680 captures owner-gone?, cancels any prior attempt, checks the predicate, and calls resolve-delay-ms.
2. timer.cljc:126-140 invokes the function-valued delay with {:snapshot snapshot}. A valid pure delay function can use rf/compute-sub against that snapshot's :data. compute-sub emits a synchronous :rf.sub/run trace (core/src/re_frame/subs.cljc:2127) before returning. A trace observer can destroy frame A and create same-id B, arming B's matching timer on that stack.
3. After resolution, timer.cljc:680-756 performs no owner check before swap! unconditionally assoc-ins A's new reservation at [frame-id k]. This overwrites B's timer entry without claiming or releasing B's handle.
4. The existing owner check at timer.cljc:819 now correctly recognizes A's loss, but it is too late: cancel-snapshotted-entry! removes A's sentinel, leaving no B entry. The overwritten B host handle is never cancelled. Its eventual callback cannot claim B's old token at timer.cljc:851 and therefore does not dispatch the timeout.

Concrete trigger / reproducible scenario
The clock is the only replaced dependency in the executed JVM witness. Frame creation/destruction, compute-sub, the trace fan-out, timer scheduling, reservation, and token claiming are real. No delay callback performs a mutation: the callback only computes from its supplied snapshot, while a synchronous tooling observer replaces the frame.

Inside machines/test-support's make-reset-runtime-fixture with plain-atom/adapter:
- Register :review/delay as (fn [db _] (:ms db)).
- Define one stable delay-fn: (fn [{:keys [snapshot]}] (rf/compute-sub [:review/delay] (:data snapshot))).
- Create :review/timer-frame A; put actor :review/timer-actor at {:state :waiting :data {:ms 5000 :rf/after-epoch {[:waiting] 1}}} under [:rf.runtime/machines :snapshots actor].
- Prepare args {:rf/parent-id actor :rf/invoke-id [:waiting] :state :waiting :delay-key delay-fn :epoch 1 :server? false}. Its timer key is {:parent actor :spawn [:waiting] :delay delay-fn}.
- Register a once-only :rf.sub/run observer for :review/delay. On its first row: destroy A; create same-id B; install B's snapshot with :ms 7000 and the same state/epoch; call timer/after-schedule-fx for B with the same args; save the resulting B entry.
- With interop/schedule-after! recording {handle, thunk, ms} and returning a distinct Object, and interop/cancel-scheduled! recording handles, call timer/after-schedule-fx for A. Then inspect B's saved/current entry and the arm/cancel logs.

Measured actual:
{:replace? true, :observer-ran? true, :armed-ms [7000], :b-was-published? true, :b-preserved? false, :live-entry-ms nil, :b-cancelled? false}
The successor really armed its 7000 ms handle and published its entry. The outer call did not arm another host timer: it erased the successor entry and aborted. B's still-scheduled host handle is no longer in the registry, so neither normal cancellation nor its token-claiming callback can finish the intended B timeout.

Expected:
B's exact saved entry/token/handle remains present and usable. A's continuation adds no reservation, handle, watcher or cancellation to B after delay resolution loses A.

Live-owner control with the observer disabled:
{:replace? false, :observer-ran? false, :armed-ms [5000], :b-was-published? false, :live-entry-ms 5000, :b-cancelled? false}
The original timer remains registered and arms exactly once.

Exact executed evidence
The full standalone witness is in the authorized ignored scratch file ai/surface-review-20260913/impl_machines/probe-impl_machines-delay-reserve-1.clj, with matching .log and .exit. Command: java -cp <existing implementation/machines/.cpcache/36AFC378842871F24A69B8CB9E79D376.cp contents> clojure.main <absolute witness path>, cwd implementation/machines. It printed the canonical source root. Exit 0 means both assertions of the observed defect and the live-owner control held; it is not a claim that the implementation passed a regression asserting desired behavior.

Suggested repair
Immediately after resolve-delay-ms returns, recheck the same owner-gone? captured before cancellation (or supplied by the hydration batch), before either the invalid-resolution shared-subscription release or the reservation/announcement branch. On loss, stop the old continuation without modifying B's timer table or decrementing a bare-id subscription ref belonging to B. Preserve the current rule that exact captured resources can be released while shared frame/query releases are skipped after owner loss. Keep reservation-before-announcement and the existing announcement-cell handoff intact; moving reservation after the trace would reintroduce rf2-jqvgp. Do not recapture an owner after resolution: that would name B and approve the stale continuation.

Acceptance criteria
- JVM and CLJS regressions replace A from a callback-bearing delay-resolution path, arm B at the identical key, and assert B's entry/token/handle are unchanged, B's callback still dispatches once, and subsequent B teardown cancels its handle normally.
- Include the pure delay-fn / compute-sub / observer case above; retain a live-owner positive control. If using a subscription path as additional coverage, assert B's held query/reaction is not decremented by A's abort.
- No A-derived timer reservation or scheduled/cancelled work is introduced into B after resolution loses the owner.
- Existing timer announce/claim, same-thread announcement replacement, hydration reconciliation, dynamic-delay re-resolution, and timer incarnation-fence controls remain green on both hosts.

Deduplication and preserved decisions
rf2-fzbj.1 is an independently actionable OPEN P1 about destroy-time exit snapshot writes and tokenless nested effects. It is separately revalidated/reused by this review; its remediation fence, status and notes are untouched. This timer defect is independent and was not a finding in that report.
Current tracker searches included machine/timer titles across all statuses, resolve-delay-ms in descriptions and notes, run-child-exit / exit-cascade descriptions, and the supplied current-issue index. The related current rf2-jqvgp is CLOSED; its current close reason and newest three history entries concern the completed reservation-before-announcement / deferred cancellation ordering fix (PR #8978). Its notes discuss cancellation and scheduled-trace replacement boundaries, not replacement during resolve-delay-ms itself. This bead preserves that completed protocol and does not reopen or undo its decision. Source provenance rf2-ijlhj has no matching current issue; do not treat that comment as a verified open owner.

Validation and limits
Confirmed by one process-local JVM witness with a live-owner control and stubbed host clock; no real wall-clock timer or persistent process was started. Separately ran five existing namespaces covering active-path geometry, raised-event FIFO, frozen region selection, announce/claim races, and hydration reconciliation: 27 tests / 143 assertions, 0 failures/errors, exit 0. That gate printed and was checked against C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2/implementation/machines; artifacts are gate-impl_machines-controls-1.log/.exit. No CLJS build/browser run, dependency install, production source edit, Git mutation, or broad gate. CLJS equivalence and the sibling invalid-subscription-resolution path are acceptance work, not additional executed claims.

title: Xray diff: preserve every removal when a multi-element vector or list becomes empty
description:
Generate valid sequential deletes when expanding a whole-vector/list replacement to empty. The current ascending synthetic indices are replayed against a shrinking sequence, so Xray omits removed values and invents surviving shifts in an ordinary clear-collection diff.

Ownership: tools/xray/**, slice tools_xray. Revision 9e8ca973767f4ecff455421e48e1765d59783261. SOURCE_ROOT=C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2; WORKTREE_ROOT=(none; read-only review). Parent rf2-gwye. P2: diagnostic diff output silently misrepresents real app-db changes.

Root cause and live consumer:
- tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/diff/engine.cljc:284-309 expands populated sequential -> empty into per-index deletes using (range (count bvec)), i.e. ascending ORIGINAL indices. The nearby comment explicitly says indices descend, but the code does the opposite.
- replay-vector-edits at 447-479 correctly applies each delete to the CURRENT evolving slot vector. After deleting index 0, the original index 1 is now at current index 0. A subsequent synthetic delete at 1 either removes the wrong original value or is skipped as out of range.
- project groups these edits at 922-977, uses replay slots for both :vector-removals and :shift-suffix, then constructs :flat-rows at 1125-1139. Thus the invalid expansion poisons both the deletion inventory and shift output.

title: False: rf2-z8ta promises shared check atoms record once, including tape expectations
description:
Merged-PR audit of #9722 (0e1d8fc2f09c23649b1a8ab86358eab69b751f72), against closed rf2-z8ta.

The new Checks paragraph in tools/story/spec/017-Testing-Story.md:1617-1623 promises that an atom shared by two checks, or by a check and terminal :assertions, dispatches and records once. That is false for the canonical tape-evaluated assertions. The terminal executor's distinct union does not govern those records: runtime.cljc:461-487 concatenates terminal, check and script atoms; plan-schema-expectations feeds that vector into result.cljc's exact-consumption matcher. The existing Schema rule explicitly preserves multiplicity (N declarations consume N violations).

Reproduced through the real plan compiler, runtime expectation collector and result matcher, with one canonical event-schema violation for :audit/submit. Register checks :check.audit/one and :check.audit/two with the same [:rf.assert/schema-error {:where :event :event :audit/submit}] atom. One check collects 1 expectation and records [:pass]. Both checks collect 2 and record [:pass :fail]. One check plus the same terminal atom also collects 2 and records [:pass :fail]. The source locations loaded by the JVM were printed and runtime.cljc/result.cljc match the landed commit; the isolated probe exited 0 with these outcomes asserted. This is a result-boundary probe, not a full browser run.

The unqualified sentence tells authors that composing those checks preserves one expectation, while the documented schema matcher requires two violations. Correct the newly added prose: limit its deduplication guarantee to atoms evaluated through the terminal executor, and explain/cross-reference the occurrence-based Schema rule for tape-evaluated schema expectations (and avoid claiming the separate causal collector deduplicates). Preserve the established exact-consumption semantics; blindly adding distinct to the collector would erase intentional repeated expectations. No public API expansion is needed.

Evidence: C:/Users/miket/.codex/tmp/audit-re-frame2-pr9722-shared-atom-probe-1.clj and its .log/.exit. All 58 literal-open Beads were searched by title, description and acceptance criteria; none records this same defect and correction. No mayor notification or acknowledgment is claimed.
acceptance_criteria: Spec 017 Checks distinguishes terminal-executor deduplication from tape-evaluated expectation collection; it no longer promises one record for shared schema-error atoms. Its explanation agrees with the existing Schema rule that two declared matching expectations require two violations. Preserve that multiset behavior, and verify the touched links/anchors with the gate that actually covers tools/story/spec.

title: [tools_support] Review: refuse editor success when auto-detect drops the requested column
description:
Recommendation: extend the editor capability refusal to detect loss of a requested column, while preserving successful line-only launches. One confirmed P2 correctness finding remains in the tools_support slice. Keep this review OPEN for that repair. The coordinator and shared Story host need no additional work from this review; testbed-support being unpublished and consumed by source paths is intentional.

## Reviewed revision and owned files

Source snapshot: 1c9ff9697b0fa3a018c7a4371e02983ad2e79b2f. HEAD when checked: 1b285ba9a841a336dd6f54f81f77aaee3150253b. `git diff --name-only <snapshot> HEAD -- <the 12 owned paths>` returned no paths; tracker-only checkpoints therefore do not change the reviewed source.

- tools/testbed-support/test/re_frame/testbed/story_host_dom_cljs_test.cljs

## Coverage and boundaries

Reviewed the tools coordinator's six local dependencies, deliberate exclusion of template resources and testbed-support, absence of retired root-level test/build coordinators, and the documentation's routing to maintained per-tool commands. Inspected neighboring tool dependency declarations, implementation/shadow-cljs.edn source paths/dev-http wiring/focused build, and implementation/package.json's test:testbed-support command. No fresh coordinator classpath defect was confirmed. Did not infer that the source-path-only support library needs a release coordinate or Story packaging dependency.

Read both implementation namespaces and the support README/spec. Followed editor admission (peer before method/preflight; Host/Origin defence in depth), query decoding, source resolution, file existence checks, process argv, timeout/termination and concurrent bounded stderr draining, position refusal, JSON response, and the client's non-2xx fallback. Inspected JVM test coverage and representative regression implementations, especially real-node capability/pipe/timeout tests; read the client fallback and host listener suites and browser teardown/handoff coverage. Followed the host's calls into Story mount/unmount. Consumer frame/image boot and frame ownership remain the caller's job, as the host contract says; the host owns one page-lifetime listener and the React-root handoff. No new host lifecycle defect was confirmed.

This is a focused inspection plus one executable process-local witness, not a full JVM/CLJS/browser test run or a claim that every owned file was executed. No build, dependency installation, application server, editor, browser, source edit, or production file mutation was performed. Existing suites' presence was inspected; their historical green results are not claimed as this review's runs.

## Finding 1 — P2: partial position loss is accepted as a successful editor launch

Owned source: tools/testbed-support/src/re_frame/testbed/open_in_editor_server.clj:187-191 (capability decision), :301-304 (exit 0 becomes success), :562-566 (success becomes HTTP 200).

Relevant promise: tools/testbed-support/spec/README.md:82-88 says HTTP 200 means the whole source coordinate reached an editor and that a position-losing launch must decline with 422 so the coordinate-preserving URI fallback runs. The column-only normalization is additionally promised at :120-123. This is a misleading success result under the existing contract, not a request to add another supported editor or implement a new editor integration.

Trigger: use the existing no-editor-hint/auto-detect route with gvim running on Linux and click a coordinate carrying a column, e.g. line 27, column 9. The installed launch-editor@2.14.1 Linux registry maps the running `gvim` process to the `gvim` command. Its get-args.js branch for `joe`/`gvim` returns `["+27", file]`: it preserves the line and discards the column. The endpoint's capability test declines only the exact bare-file vector `["F"]`, so this line-only argv passes. If the editor command exits successfully, the endpoint returns 200 and core's fetch-launcher! suppresses URI fallback. A column-only request is normalized to line 1 and also loses its requested column while returning 200.

Other installed get-args.js line-only cases (`rmate`/`mate`/`mine`, and `joe`) show the same capability distinction, but gvim is sufficient: it is directly reachable through an existing auto-detection registry. The report does not depend on supporting those additional names.

Expected: when a requested column cannot reach the launcher argv, return the existing 422/editor-position-unsupported result before launching, allowing the existing client fallback. Continue to accept gvim requests that ask only for a line, because that coordinate is preserved. Continue to accept position-capable commands.

Actual executable result through the real handler and original shim:
- Synthetic Linux auto-detect gvim, requested [27 9]: actual dependency invocation verified as ["+27", file]; HTTP 200, {"ok":true,"file":file}.
- Same gvim, requested [nil 9]: invocation ["+1", file]; HTTP 200.
- Positive control gvim, requested [27 nil]: invocation ["+27", file]; HTTP 200.
- Positive control code, requested [27 9]: invocation ["-r","-g",file+":27:9"]; HTTP 200.
- Existing refusal control Brackets, requested [27 9]: HTTP 422/editor-position-unsupported, no editor spawn.

Impact: a source-chip click appears successful but lands at an incorrect column; the truthful fallback is prevented by the false success. This is the same user-visible success/fallback invariant as the earlier total-position-loss repair, reached through a different dependency branch.

Reproducer and validation detail:
1. Load `re-frame.testbed.open-in-editor-server` from the reviewed absolute source root on a JVM using the already-cached testbed-support classpath; save the original value of its private launch-shim.
2. Set the JVM process-local user.dir to the implementation directory so Node resolves the installed launch-editor. For each test, prepend a safety/witness shim to the original launch-shim with with-redefs. The prefix clears LAUNCH_EDITOR/VISUAL/EDITOR in that Node process, sets process.platform to linux, replaces child_process.execSync with a synthetic `gvim\n` process listing, and replaces child_process.spawn with an EventEmitter stub. The spawn stub verifies the exact expected editor/argv (exits 71 on mismatch), then emits a successful exit; unexpected child_process.exec exits 72. No real editor can launch.
3. Call the real handler with uri=/__rf-open-in-editor, request-method=:post, remote-addr=127.0.0.1, Host=localhost:8031, Origin=http://localhost:8031, and query `file=<existing absolute reviewed source file>&line=27&column=9` (no editor hint). Repeat the four controls above. The original launch-editor package performs guessing, get-args selection, file parsing, and launch composition; only platform/process-list inputs and the final editor spawn are synthetic.
4. The witness exits 0 only when all five observed outcomes above match. It prints the loaded endpoint resource URL, which was file:/C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2/tools/testbed-support/src/re_frame/testbed/open_in_editor_server.clj. Review artifacts, all verified ignored: ai/surface-review-20260912/probe-tools-support-editor-1.clj, probe-tools-support-editor-1.log, probe-tools-support-editor-1.exit. Captured process exit: 0. This means the counterexample and controls reproduced, not that the contract passed. JVM and its five bounded Node children completed; shutdown-agents was called.

Precise repair recommendation: extend the existing dependency capability question to distinguish preservation of each requested coordinate component. A small differential check of get-args output for two distinct column values, holding a sentinel file and line fixed, can detect a column-insensitive branch without inventing another editor registry. When a column is requested and the generated argv is unchanged, return the existing unsupported-position exit/result before launch. Keep the current line-only/no-coordinate behavior, named-editor vocabulary, endpoint/fallback architecture, and process lifecycle unchanged. Do not add a second editor launcher or broaden this into general editor support.

Acceptance criteria:
1. A real-package, synthetic-process/spawn regression through launch! or handler proves gvim with [27 9] and [nil 9] is refused before editor spawn with 422/editor-position-unsupported; restoring the current `["F"]`-only predicate makes it fail.
2. Gvim [27 nil] and coordinate-free launches still reach the launcher; code/zed/idea with both components still carry both and remain eligible for success. Brackets/Windsurf refusal regressions remain intact.
3. Extend capability-test assertions to prove column survival where promised, not only line presence or argv != ["F"]. The existing real-package vocabulary assertion at open_in_editor_server_test.clj:1308-1317 checks for line 27 but never for column 9.
4. Existing non-2xx client fallback coverage continues to prove one fallback with the requested coordinate. Run the focused JVM testbed-support lane with RF2_REQUIRE_NODE_PROBES set and the focused CLJS client suite appropriate to any changes. No browser UI redesign is needed.

## Related history and duplicate check

All-status title/description searches for testbed-support/editor/column were checked, then relevant current closure records were read. rf2-1i1ec is CLOSED: it repaired Windsurf/auto-detected bare-file launches and later the column-only request skipping the probe entirely. The current predicate does execute for this finding; it accepts a non-bare argv that has lost only the column. This remaining partial-loss defect is distinct from that closed outcome. Its original success invariant corroborates the local spec, but this finding is established against current source and a new witness.

Other related closed work inspected: rf2-mpgs (actual TCP-peer boundary), rf2-6r9j.116 (DOM fixture unregisters its exact listener), rf2-cl8mg (real-node CI probes no longer silently skip when armed), rf2-3xq1v (checkout-root retirement/source-coordinate fallback), and rf2-6r9j.139/.140 (retired duplicate tools-root test/build coordinators). These repairs are reflected in the inspected code and are not re-filed here.

## Explicit limits / unverified risks

No real Linux desktop, gvim process, editor GUI, browser fallback navigation, complete JVM suite, or CLJS compilation was run. Linux auto-detection and successful editor exit were synthetic inputs in Windows-hosted Node; installed dependency argument construction and the JVM response mapping were real. This is sufficient to prove the inaccurate accepted argv/result contract, not physical editor behavior. No separate speculative process-hardening, malformed-input minutia, or documentation cosmetics are promoted as defects. Root owns tracker checkpoint/push; this worker made no source/build changes.

title: [examples/real-apps] Repair comment validation, feed settlement/invalidation, and stale article-write continuations
description:
Recommendation: repair four application correctness defects before using the RealWorld examples as worked guidance: make optimistic comments conform to their durable schema, correlate home-feed replies with the selected feed, invalidate the session feed after follow changes, and prevent departed-page write continuations from overwriting the reader's newer work/navigation. These are concrete runtime gaps, not requests for a framework redesign or a new example test suite. Keep the existing HTTP-versus-Resources architecture comparison and keep examples test-free.

Verdict: four confirmed P2 defects; remediation remains, so this review bead stays OPEN. Exactly one bead is filed for the examples_real_apps slice.

SOURCE_ROOT=C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2
WORKTREE_ROOT=(none; read-only review)
Reviewed revision: 1c9ff9697b0fa3a018c7a4371e02983ad2e79b2f. HEAD was rechecked at the end; git diff under examples/real-apps was empty. No source edits, checkout, build, server, dependency install, commit or push was performed. The parent reviewer handles tracker checkpoint/push.

## Confirmed finding 1 — P2: normal optimistic comment submission is rejected by the HTTP app's development schema

Owned source: examples/real-apps/realworld_http/schema.cljs:257-258,266-267; realworld_http/comments.cljs:192-195,391-428; realworld_shared/schema.cljs:120-127 (all under examples/real-apps).

Trigger: run the HTTP example in the documented development mode, sign in, open an article, enter a nonblank comment, and click Post Comment. The recordable :realworld/temp-comment-id supplier returns a string beginning with temp-. :comment-form/submit inserts that string as :id in the optimistic comment and returns the POST effect. The production app registers [:comments :data] as [:maybe [:vector ws/Comment]], but the wire Comment schema requires :id :int.

Expected: the temporary comment commits and its POST is sent; the successful integer-id server comment subsequently replaces it. Actual: the pending app-db candidate fails its registered schema at the comment's :id. Current core commit-and-flow! rejects both the db transition and its fx, so the comment never appears and no POST is sent. Production validation elision hides the mismatch; this is an immediate failure in the normal development build.

Executed evidence: review-examples-real-apps-schema-2.clj reads/evaluates the actual shared schema definitions, actual app-db-schemas definition, actual HTTP request builder, and actual comment-submit reducer. A process-local plain-atom frame registers the exact production [:comments :data] schema. A small wrapper supplies the route and recordable temp-id coeffect, then dispatches through current core and schemas with cached Malli 0.20.1. Output: before-valid true; candidate-valid false; error :in [0 :id], value temp-probe; after dispatch comments [], HTTP calls 0. The same source reducer with an integer temp-id control commits the comment and records HTTP calls 1. This is a core/schema integration probe, not a browser run.

Repair: define the application's durable comment shape to admit its explicit temporary-ID representation, or generate a suitable integer temporary ID. Preserve the strict integer-ID wire decode schema. Do not disable validation or widen every server ID to :any.

Acceptance: in the existing external RealWorld harness, register the production app schemas on the tested frame and exercise the real comment-form event with its normal string supplier. Assert one optimistic card, one POST, then replacement by the real server ID; failure must remove the optimistic card and leave a usable form. Keep a wire-schema control rejecting string server comment IDs if the repair uses a separate durable shape.

Coverage gap explaining existing green: implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/realworld_cljs_test.cljs:3601-3655 runs its production-backend receipt on an anonymous frame without registering the app's comments schema. The same test file already documents this exact instrumentation distinction for AuthSlice at :258-310; the comment receipt does not inherit schemas registered for :rf/default.

## Confirmed finding 2 — P2: an old feed reply permanently settles the HTTP home machine for the new feed

Owned source: examples/real-apps/realworld_http/tags.cljs:250-276; realworld_http/articles.cljs:115-160,261-286,345-361,544-549; realworld_http/favorites.cljs:80-105.

Trigger: while signed in, start loading Your Feed, switch to Global Feed before the first request settles, let the old empty Your Feed response arrive, then let the nonempty Global Feed response arrive. This is a normal sequence against the shipped demo world's initially empty following feed; a held-transport reproduction makes the reply order deterministic.

Expected: Global Feed settles from its own response and displays its articles. Actual: both :feed/loaded and :articles/loaded emit the same uncorrelated [:realworld/articles-home [:fetch-succeeded ...]]. The two request families use different stable IDs (:feed/load versus :articles/load), and :home/load neither cancels the departed family nor correlates its machine signal. The old empty response transitions the shared data region to :empty. :empty has no :fetch-succeeded transition, so the new Global Feed success is ignored by the machine even though it installs the articles in app-db. The view continues to render the empty-feed state. Stable IDs only supersede requests within each family.

Executed evidence: review-examples-real-apps-probe-2.clj reads the actual home-machine definition and actual loaded handlers, feeds their actual emitted events through the current re-frame.machines.parallel/machine-transition implementation, then calls the actual :articles.home/render selector. Result: :state {:data :empty :feed :global :filter :none}, render :empty, app-db global data [{:slug "hello-conduit"}]. Removing the old reply from the identical sequence gives render :some. The reverse ordering of empty global/tag response versus populated following feed also reproduced.

Repair: give the shared home lifecycle one active request/selection identity, or carry a feed/selection identity on success and failure callbacks and reject departed selections before emitting machine signals. Canceling the outgoing family can be cleanup, but already-queued replies still need correct ownership. Keep same-feed request supersession and pagination semantics.

Acceptance: use held production HTTP requests in the existing external harness for Your Feed -> Global Feed and the reverse; release old success/error before and after the active response, with empty/nonempty contrasts. The current feed alone controls busy/error/empty/render state, and a normal current success still renders its data.

## Confirmed finding 3 — P2: Resources follow/unfollow leaves a fresh cached Your Feed unchanged

Owned source: examples/real-apps/realworld_resources/mutations.cljs:214-237; realworld_resources/resources.cljs:41-45,274-295; realworld_resources/views.cljs:121-129,142-185,381-409; realworld_resources/routing.cljs:103-109.

Trigger: sign in, visit Your Feed to cache its empty result, visit stub-bot's profile or article, follow the author, then return to Your Feed within the 60-second freshness window. Reverse with unfollow after caching a populated feed.

Expected: the successful relationship mutation makes that user's personalized feed stale, and returning to it fetches the changed membership. Actual: both follow mutations invalidate only #{[:profile username]} in {:from-db :realworld/viewer}. The feed belongs to {:from-db :realworld/session} and carries [:feed] plus per-article tags. No scope/tag target matches it. Article-page follow adds only a viewer-scoped [:article slug] invalidation. The backend changes its :following set, but the still-fresh feed is reused unchanged on re-entry.

Executed/source evidence: actual :invalidates functions and actual feed :tags function were evaluated from source. Both mutations returned only the viewer/profile descriptor; the empty feed tags were #{[:feed]}, its scope was the session resolver, and matching descriptors counted 0. Framework source confirms the meaning: implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/events.cljc:436-439 skips a loaded fresh entry, and state.cljc:762-778 defines freshness from invalidation/stale-at. The shared demo backend's transition updates following at demo_backend.cljs:532-535 and computes feed membership from it at :433-436. No browser/cache-runtime sequence was executed for this finding; the descriptor mismatch and freshness path were evaluated/inspected directly.

Repair: add the session-scoped #{[:feed]} invalidation to both follow and unfollow mutations, using the same explicit cross-scope descriptor style already used by favorite mutations. Keep profile population and the existing article-detail refresh behavior.

Acceptance: warm an empty feed, follow an author, re-enter before stale-after-ms and assert a new fetch plus the author's articles; warm a populated feed, unfollow, re-enter and assert removal. Cover both profile and article follow entry points, and retain the profile :populates control. Do not make every route force-refresh to mask the missing invalidation.

## Confirmed finding 4 — P2: departed-page article write continuations can replace newer drafts/routes

Owned source: examples/real-apps/realworld_http/article_editor.cljs:430-480; realworld_resources/article_editor.cljs:405-469; realworld_resources/views.cljs:188-212.

Concrete triggers:
- HTTP editor: open an existing clean article, click Delete and hold its reply; navigate to New Article, type a new draft, then release the old delete success. :editor/delete-success replaces the entire editor slice with a blank one before navigating home. The new draft is lost and the subsequent leave guard sees the already-cleared draft. The old save-success path likewise installs its returned article and navigates without a captured editor owner.
- Resources editor: click Delete on a clean edit page, navigate to a profile while the mutation is pending, then release success. :editor/replied clears the editor and navigates home regardless of the new route.
- Resources article detail: click Delete, navigate to a different article or profile, release success. :ui/article-deleted always navigates home. Its call site does not even carry the originating slug on the reply target.

Expected: the server write may finish, but it must not overwrite another editing session or redirect a reader who has left the initiating page. Actual: these handlers check at most reply status and do not test current route/editor ownership. A route-owned resource read being released does not retire the independent mutation continuation.

Executed evidence: actual source reply functions were evaluated with the current route set to profile/eve and a newer editor draft. HTTP and Resources editor success functions returned replacement editor state plus navigation; both delete functions returned title "" and home navigation, and both save functions returned the old saved article plus article navigation. The Resources detail-delete function returned clear-instance plus home navigation on the newer profile route. The Resources new-editor entry does clear :editor/save and can suppress that specific old-instance path; the supported Resources reproducer therefore uses a detour to a profile, not a claim that an old cleared mutation survives entering a new editor. HTTP resets only its UI machine/slice, so the new-draft loss is a distinct reachable path there.

Repair: capture an originating page/edit operation identity in write continuation targets and gate page-local db writes/navigation against it; retire or reset per-editor pending state on a new editing session without stranding controls. Preserve server/cache reconciliation where it is still valid and preserve same-page save/delete success. The existing HTTP article-detail article-route-for-slug? predicate is the simple precedent for route-owned navigation; a nil/new draft or a replaced editing session needs its own identity, not only a cached slug comparison.

Acceptance: in the existing external harnesses, hold real writes, perform the above navigations, release success/error, and assert no stale redirect or newer-draft mutation. Specifically preserve the HTTP new draft after the old Delete succeeds; cover Resources detail alpha -> beta and alpha -> profile/eve, and Resources editor -> profile/eve. Retain positive current-owner save/delete behavior and usable controls after refusing a stale completion.

## Prior work and duplicate check

Searched active and closed bead titles/descriptions for RealWorld, real-apps, follow invalidation, feed races/cross-feed replies, late editor completion, and temporary-comment/schema mismatches; read relevant source/history. No existing task covers these four confirmed defects. Relevant resolved precedents remain resolved:
- rf2-amhpk fixed HTTP ARTICLE-DETAIL delete navigation by checking the current route. Its close reason explicitly excludes :editor/delete-success. Current comments.cljs:625-642 contains that fix. Its latest history snapshots were checked as closed. Finding 4 covers the different editor and Resources paths, not reopening that fix.
- rf2-iy3d6, rf2-84iek and rf2-8icg cover article/comments cross-slug and profile cross-username correlations. Their current guards/reset behavior was inspected; neither owns the shared home feed machine.
- rf2-2ape covers settings replies after logout/account switch. Current session-owner checks were inspected; this review does not broaden its intentional same-session settings continuation semantics.
- rf2-9n43e and rf2-k5lbd established the stateful backend and production-seam receipts. Finding 3 is missing client cache invalidation against a backend that now correctly persists follows.
- rf2-0mxz fixed tag normalization in the Resources editor; the current one-parse boundary was inspected.
- rf2-2xzc/rf2-ghxt cover boot-window schema failures. Finding 1 is a later optimistic-comment candidate mismatch, not the already-fixed nullable boot slices.
- rf2-do50/rf2-pxzf are the known host-page base-path fixes; their close reasons were read rather than treating the existing base tag as a new finding.
- Historical rf2-czvc is referenced by git commits 3324246dcb and d8bf3be425 for editor GET correlation/leafwise seeding. bd show no longer resolves that identity. The current fixes concern article reads, not the write continuations in finding 4.

## Coverage and validation limits

Inspected both apps' boot/frame initialization, bearer request decoration, auth machine/form/session flows, schema attachments, route/query/page wiring and auth/dirty guards, home/tag/feed machines or resource plans, article/comment/favorite/follow flows, profile tabs, settings, editors, and subscription/render decisions. Inspected the shared stateful demo transition, wire schemas, query/retry/failure helpers, markdown sanitization, avatar fallback, host-page assets, and HTTP SSR payload helper. Followed neighboring resource freshness/mutation continuation and core validation/machine engine sources, plus relevant external RealWorld tests and build declarations. This is substantive source coverage, not a claim every page was executed.

Executed only focused process-local Babashka probes against the stated checkout using existing source and cached dependencies. Evidence under ignored ai/surface-review-20260912:
- review-examples-real-apps-probe-1.log / .exit: exit 0; handler, mutation-descriptor, and machine-engine counterexamples.
- review-examples-real-apps-probe-2.log / .exit: exit 0; adds the ordinary empty-Your-Feed -> Global-Feed ordering and actual render-selector control.
- review-examples-real-apps-schema-1.log / .exit: exit 1, a probe setup error (no adapter installed), not a product verdict.
- review-examples-real-apps-schema-2.log / .exit: exit 0 after installing the repository's plain-atom adapter; genuine core/schema rejection and positive effect control.
Every successful witness prints SOURCE_ROOT=C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2, and source-derived counterexamples/controls discriminate the reviewed definitions. No shared compiler output was used or generated. No broad gate, CLJS compile, full test suite, browser/React mount, external API call, visual/accessibility audit, deployment check, or exhaustive failure permutation was run. Examples deliberately contain no local specs; their absence is not a defect. Potential issues outside the four confirmed findings were not promoted into speculative requirements.
